stem: Muttley Magee is an 8-year-old boy with asthma. He has had asthma attacks every month over winter and was discharged from the paediatric intensive care unit a few days ago after a severe attack. He has been off oxygen since yesterday. He has also been waking at night at least 5 days every week, has wheeze with exercise, and needs salbutamol (Ventolin) at least once a day. If symptoms get worse, what preventer and dose would you prescribe?

options.text: Flixotide junior (50mcg) 2 puffs BD
Flixotide junior (50mcg) 2 puffs twice per day
Seretide 125 mcg 1 puff BD
Seretide 125 mcg 1 puff twice per day
Seretide 250 mcg 1 puff BD
Seretide 250 mcg 1 puff twice per day
Flixotide junior (50mcg) 4 puffs BD
Flixotide junior (50mcg) 4 puffs twice per day

explanation: This child has very poorly controlled asthma with frequent daytime symptoms, frequent night waking, exercise limitation, frequent reliever use, and a recent severe exacerbation requiring PICU. A higher-step preventer is appropriate; among the listed options, Seretide 125 mcg 1 puff twice daily is the best match.
rationale: The item is answerable with the existing options. 'BD' and 'twice per day' are equivalent; only one option should be marked correct, so the best existing choice is D.

optionExplanations.A: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid alone; insufficient for this level of poor control.
optionExplanations.B: Duplicate wording of option A; still too low a step.
optionExplanations.C: Combined preventer but the dose is less suitable than the best option listed.
optionExplanations.D: Best option listed for severe uncontrolled asthma in this child.
optionExplanations.E: Higher dose than needed as first choice among the listed options.
optionExplanations.F: Too high a dose among the listed options.
optionExplanations.G: Higher-dose inhaled corticosteroid alone, but combination therapy is preferred here.
optionExplanations.H: Duplicate wording of option G; dose is not the best match.
